source: Built deterministically from liraasa_3_1.json (sha256 55bb28c486ed61fb64f466d6b38193b2c8829f47d91a68a6e8047374ab15ed3f) by scripts/integrate_3_3.ts, applying the changeset 2026-10-25-lexicon-3-3-ratify-3-1 and 2026-10-25-lexicon-3-3 (ADR-0023). This JSON is the single source of truth for Liraasa 3.3. PROPOSED: every 3.0 and 3.3 addition (3.1 is ratified) awaits the author's ratification.

phonology.vowels: a e i o u (pure); adjacent vowels are separate syllables
phonology.consonants_core: l m n r s v y
phonology.consonants_other: b d p t g h z k c f j (sh, ch only in colour/number words)
phonology.new_root_template: two syllables, consonant-initial, vowel-final, letters from the inventory, no initial cluster (kr-, tr- grandfathered), no three-consonant cluster, no doubled letter, at least two edits from every active word
phonology.function_word_template: one to three syllables, vowel-final, no initial cluster; at least two edits from every active word; monosyllables may sit one edit from another monosyllable only if they belong to different syntactic positions (declared list)
protected_exceptions: 39 amor compounds (legacy canon): 20 ending -amor, 19 beginning amor-

morphology.compounding: MODIFIER+HEAD written together; head rightmost; components must be active headwords (a colour base may be the modifier, 2.0:G38; a component may itself be a compound, 2.0:G42); a compound's verb class follows its first letter

derivation_defaults.-yo: one who does R; one devoted to R
derivation_defaults.-ti: a little or dear R (also affectionate)
derivation_defaults.constraints: one form OR one derivation, then -ti, then -ri (unchanged). Prefer a listed derivation when one exists.

lexicalised_diminutives.miruralnoti: trickle; a drip of water: miruralno + -ti

image_compounds.name: Image compounds
image_compounds.rule: MODIFIER + HEAD, written as one word, where MODIFIER is any root in 'modifiers' and HEAD any root in 'heads'. Meaning: '<modifier adjective> <head>', that is, <head template> <modifier sense>. Example: luno + savali = lunosavali, 'moonlit kiss; an intimate kiss recalling moonlight'. Every such pair is valid Liraasa and needs no 'new' flag. Verb class follows the first letter, as for all compounds.
image_compounds.why: 394 dictionary entries followed this exact pattern. Listing them added size but no expressive power, and implied that unlisted pairs (moonlit voice, rain-washed promise) were less valid. As a pattern, all 57 x 31 = 1,767 pairs are available.

rulings_1_0.ruling: Every preverbal operator scopes over everything to its right. Pre-constituent operators (ne, doli, tu, yesta, pendi, vinto) scope over the single constituent that follows them.
si means only 'if'. 'whether' is ki-oro. 0.8 texts that used si for 'whether' are read under 0.8 rules.
povi = ability; nosi = epistemic possibility (might); dagi = permission (may, be allowed). 0.8's double use of nosi is split.
'must (logically)' = inferential evidential tosu + seye; musi is only obligation or circumstantial necessity.
Intent is the verb chain 'dorvada sidu VERB' (intend to); kopi is only 'hope to'. Deliberately = la dorvasan; accidentally = la dorvanasan.
noma marks a clause as contrary to fact. 'should have' = po noma suvi; 'could have' = po noma povi; 'would have' = po viki (in a consequence clause) or po noma viki.
fututi in the approach slot means 'about to': Maivo po fututi pagopa = I was about to leave. As a clause-initial time word it still means 'soon'.
loki covers both 'still' and 'keep on'; no separate continuative is added.
Before a number or quantity, lusu = at least, mosa = at most, gase = approximately; pendi = exactly.
oro A oro B = either A or B; ne A ne B = neither A nor B; doli si = only if; yesta si = even if; 'si …, ata doli si …' = if and only if.
nevi + noun phrase = despite: nevi li zeldo, despite the resistance. nevi + clause = although.
vobi + noun phrase = for the benefit of / on behalf of (unchanged), and combines with any operator.
ata is 'and' only; additive 'also' is tu.

vaku (make), lesvu (let) and tekvu (prevent) fill the verb slot of the main clause; the actor follows, then the actor's own [ne] [phase] [effort] verb. Tense, modal and evidential belong to the main clause only.
ne before an operator negates the operator; ne after it negates the event: po ne vazdi lirala = didn't manage to sing; po vazdi ne lirala = managed not to sing.

At most one word per slot. hiro/teki do not combine with roni or tefa. tavki excludes fututi (same slot). The effort slot (telvo, vazdi, fesmo) excludes tefa. noma requires a tense, modal or si-clause context.
la vuzinasan = unexpectedly; kroti ola = previously; nayo ola = meanwhile/simultaneously; krotiapo = subsequently. No new words.
A hozi-topic opens the clause; vinto may then mark a focus inside it. hozi and vinto never mark the same constituent.
Texts dated before 1.0 are interpreted with the 0.8 lexicon and rules. A 1.0 reader meeting a retired spelling looks it up in legacy.retired and reads the 1.0 replacement.
tisebitivu (sword), tibivu (rope), kaldopago (prison) and zeldoyo (rebel) are fixed meanings of regular derivations.

A raho-clause that does not end the sentence is closed by a comma in writing and a pause in speech: Li sabeyo raho vismava eli, ne yehu vimova li vordu. (Found in stress-testing: without the pause the main verb is read inside the relative clause.)
seye, mufe, poye, pifu and zoke never open a clause. 'Perhaps, …' at the start of a sentence is written with the clause-final poye. (Found in stress-testing.)
venreva (come) with an event as subject means 'take place, happen': Li dapadonu po venreva kroti li foji, the sale took place before winter.

rulings_0_8_carried.ruling: The JSON is authoritative; the workbook is generated. Language field and files are named Liraasa.
An unused form may receive a gloss only when its compositional meaning is predictable, approved case by case, and recorded in authorized_changes.
Frozen for 0.8. No canonical root is respelled; the 40-root queue carries forward unchanged.

A standalone tense particle opening a paragraph or turn (Po — / Futu —) sets a frame: following unmarked main clauses take that tense until another tense particle, pressa, or the end of the paragraph. Optional. Time words do not set a frame, so 0.7 texts keep their meaning.
li may be omitted in everyday speech as well as verse when the referent is obvious; never when ambiguous. baba may be omitted only in verse.
sige clauses never inherit tense; they are always marked. Tense inheritance applies to fime, raho, kube, nayo, kasa, kopisa and tuni.
deyaapo is kept as a fossil (it retains the retired past marker apo). apo is not used in new compounds; say vesno de deyaapo.
amorliraa, amorrinbaa and amorvulraa are correct; each a is its own syllable.
A certainty marker (or zoke) precedes ki: Taivo lirala poye ki?
Registers are defined in the grammar guide. The lexicon keeps everyday and poetic labels; sacred is added only to headwords whose root meaning is inherently sacred, after review.
New vocabulary is sized by genuine gaps, not by the 120-150 target.
The diminutive -ti may attach to personal names as an affectionate or teasing form (Dorinti).

eli/ola (and eliri/olari) stand alone for things, situations and discourse (ola = what was just said; eli = what follows). For people use eli-nela/ola-nela or saivo, except presentational Eli ka NAME.

ne precedes what it negates: verb or modal (after tense), copula (ne ka), noun phrase or fragment (Ne eli), or a contrasted constituent (ne X, nara Y). Negation is compositional: ne + nuna- is a positive (avoid).

Everyday speech may omit a repeated subject in coordinated clauses and in answers, omit a repeated predicate after a contrasting subject (Dorin, ne.), answer with tense + verb (Po sapusia.), and echo a word with ki. Speech may break off after any particle; the listener may complete it.

ki may close the main clause before an appended direct quotation (Taivo desida ki, fime maivo senosia: "...") as well as after it (0.7 order). Embedded wh-questions keep the wh-word in place with no ki; embedded yes/no questions use si (whether).
Inside an inheriting clause: tefa marks prior action, nayo/roni simultaneous, futu subsequent (future-in-past), sahi habitual.

The root (form 1) is the noun of action or thing (juba, donu, tali). A verb phrase becomes a noun phrase with sidu (Sidu lisrola ka livna de taivo) or a clause with fime (Fime taivo po relnura ka baba juba).
[toda|rada|muya|poka|somi|nuna] [li|eli|ola|OWNER de] [NUMBER] [ADJ...] NOUN[-ti][-ri] [de ...] [raho ...]. toda N = every N; toda li N = all the N; toda OWNER de N = all OWNER's N.
X ka sambasan ko Y (same as); X ka sambanasan da Y (different from); gase NP alone = like NP (simile); gase ADJ gase NP = as ADJ as NP. Lotero silda, ... = on the other hand.

rulings_1_2.ruling: A time word or time correlative (eli-krono, deyapressa, fututi, ki-krono's answers…) may open its clause or close it. When it opens the clause, the comma after it is optional. Only the four frame words zafra, finra, lanto and kenvi are opening-only, and they keep their comma.

A single oro joins two equal constituents, exactly as ata does: miru oro nami, water or food. It may also open a clause or line that continues the one before ("Or …"). The pair oro A oro B is the emphatic "either A or B".
examples: oro maivo ke li suma ki?

rulings_1_2.topic: Give-type verbs: where the recipient goes
rulings_1_2.ruling: A verb of giving (give, lend, send, owe, sell, pay, bring, teach, show) takes VERB THEME ala RECIPIENT. When the recipient is a pronoun it may instead stand bare straight after the verb: VERB PRONOUN THEME. Any other recipient takes ala.
examples: Fisa, rimara tressa cono ala maivo.

rulings_1_2.topic: Which side of de is the owner
rulings_1_2.ruling: In X de Y the owner is Y, read as English "X of Y": li bumre de li cilni, the bread of the city; li lira de amor, the song of love. One exception: a pronoun or a personal name (pilo, father, used as a name included) standing before de is the owner, read as English "X's Y": maivo de lira, my song; pilo de bumre, father's bread. A pronoun is the owner wherever it stands: li purma de maivo, my parent. Fractions (tressa de cuara) are their own construction.
examples: Li bitiri de pilo ke su li tabu.
Father's tools are on the table.
Eli bumre ka sambasan ko pilo de bumre.
This bread is the same as father's bread.
Li bumre de li cilni ka sambanasan da eli bumre.
City bread is different from this bread.
Nullo de deyaapo, maivo po ne somusia.

rulings_1_2.ruling: After a number or a quantifier the plural -ri is optional: the number already says how many. Choose by sound and meter. Without a number or quantifier, a plural noun takes -ri.
examples: Maivo po vimova muya zimziri en li folni.
I saw many insects on the flower.

rulings_1_2.topic: An adjective standing as a noun
rulings_1_2.ruling: An adjective may stand as a noun phrase on its own only after an article or determiner (li, eli, ola, baba): li ramumomvisan, the forgotten. Without one, an adjective needs its noun.
examples: yesta li raleri de li sadori de li ramumomvisan po lenila maivori de lira.
even the echoes of the sorrows of the forgotten heard our song

rulings_1_2.ruling: Liraasa has no word for "about / concerning". A song, story or word about something is a de phrase under G27: li lira de amor, the song of (about) love. After a verb of saying, give the verb an object rather than su: po sarbisia lirari de amor, wrote songs of love.
examples: Li ralelirapatu de li lira ka melosan.
Li veluri po sarbisia lirari de amor.
The stars wrote songs of love.

rulings_1_2.ruling: A command has no subject: the clause opens at the verb (slot 3 notes), softened with fisa. A person addressed is a noun phrase set off by commas, at the start or end of the clause. In verse, once the time has been set, the bare present may narrate past events.
examples: Taivo viki pagopa ligo maivo ki, maivo de amor?
Would you come near me, my love?

rulings_1_2.ruling: When de joins two candidates for owner, the owner is decided in this order: a pronoun, then a personal name (pilo, mare used as names included), then the default of 1.2:G27 (in X de Y, Y is the owner). Pilo de maivo is my father, not father's me. PRONOUN de PRONOUN is allowed, and the right-hand pronoun is the owner: taivo de maivo, you of mine.

yuta + noun phrase names the instrument or means of an action: with, using, by means of. It fills the ADJUNCTS slot like the other prepositions. It never means accompaniment: "with a friend" stays ko.
examples: Maivo lallela li dorbi yuta li kemye.
I open the door with the key.
Li lirayo po yugemeyiya saivo yuta melo.
The singer healed him with music.
Saivori po ka vazranasan yuta benamolu.

rulings_1_2.ruling: A quantifier joined to krono with a hyphen gives a frequency adverbial: muya-krono often, poka-krono rarely, rada-krono each time. Like the other -krono correlatives it opens or closes its clause (1.2:G24). The pattern is limited to krono; muya, poka and rada form no other correlatives.
revo-sabesia (know again: recognize) and yave-donuda (give together: share) join revo-vimova and revo-lirala as curated metaphors. The motion prefixes otherwise stay non-productive.

Kinship words are neutral: purma parent, famli sibling, linu child, purmafamli aunt or uncle. Gender is marked only when it matters, by a compound with minva (female) or tarnu (male) where the lexicon has one (minvalinu daughter, tarnufamli brother), and otherwise by the adjective before the noun (minvasan purmafamli, aunt). mare and pilo remain mother and father. Kin by marriage compound with rilde: rildemare mother-in-law. Neither gender root is the negative of the other.
examples: Li tarnufamli de taivo ka corvisan.

rulings_2_0.ruling: Declare devo / devi and nevi / devi as permitted one-edit pairs.

rulings_2_0.topic: Colour bases in compounds; compounds lexicalised with -ti
rulings_2_0.ruling: Colour bases may act as the modifier in a dictionary compound, and a compound may be lexicalised with -ti.
aurumijuba and vanajuba become dictionary headwords as well as colour words.
Image compounds: any listed modifier + any listed head is a valid word with a predictable meaning, no 'new' flag needed (see pattern_compounds).

Derivations are fully productive with default readings: R+yo = one who does R, or one devoted to R; R+vu = a big or intense R; R+pago = the place of R; R+ti = a little or dear R. They attach to any root or compound (as lemudonuyo and mambicuzayo already do). Listed derivations keep their fixed meanings and override the default.

A compound may take a compound as one of its two parts: MODIFIER + HEAD still joins exactly two headwords, either of which may itself be a compound (larbopago + safa = larbopagosafa). 1.2 avoided nesting; 2.0 allows it.

Vowels are pure, as in Spanish or Italian. l m n s v b d p t f k sound as in English; y as in "yes"; r is a single tap, as in Spanish "pero"; g is always hard, as in "go"; h as in "hope"; z as in "zone". c is always "ch" as in "chant", before every vowel: ca = cha, co = cho, and likewise ce, ci, cu. j is the voiced partner of c, as in "jewel". sh is as in "shade"; ch, written only in a few colour and number words, is the same sound as c.

Every written vowel is its own syllable (0.8:R8), but in singing neighbouring vowels may glide into one note: benaasa may be sung be-na-a-sa or be-naa-sa. The spelling never changes; the songwriter chooses the count the melody needs.
A foreign name is not translated. It is copied as closely as Liraasa letters allow, choosing among near spellings by how the name sounds and sings.

rulings_2_1.topic: Questions keep every word in place
rulings_2_1.ruling: A question word stands where its answer would stand; every direct question ends in ki. A ki-word of time may open the clause as a frame. Embedded questions unchanged (0.8:G4, 1.0:G2). Replaces the fronted small-words examples: Taivo pagopa ki-pago ki?
A main clause with a ki-word and no final ki is an exclamation (!). ki-modo + ADJ = how ...!; ki-eli + N = what a ...!; ki-muya + N = so many ...! Li nullo ka ki-modo vanisan!
pifu with any subject is the blessing form: Li lumi tivrota taivo pifu. noma + pifu = if only: Taivo po noma lisrola pifu.
NUMBER-krono = N times (una-krono once, dossa-krono twice); ki-muya-krono = how many times; una-ne krono = the first time; una-krono never means formerly (somi-krono).
A second verb with its own subject goes in a fime clause: Maivo desida fime taivo lisrola. sidu stays same-subject; fime inherits tense (0.8:R6).
No evidential = no claim about source. Inside fime, the evidential reports the main-clause subject's evidence. In a question it asks the listener's source.
raho opens the clause; the preposition keeps its place with a resumptive pronoun (ito/itori, saivo/saivori): Li nimu raho maivo po lirala en ito, ka vanisan.
After a number, quantifier, or superlative, de means of/among and G27/G32 ownership does not apply: Una de maivori futu relnura. Fractions are the same construction.
ola-modo + ADJ ... fime CLAUSE = so ADJ that: Taivo ke ola-modo vanisan fime li veluri lasola.
Bare measure after the object = duration; kroti + measure (no article) = ago; krotiapo + measure = in/after. kroti/krotiapo + li + noun = before/after it.
ne + command, no subject; fisa softens; yava ne + verb = let us not.

Guidance for new and respelled roots: prefer CVCV; l m n r v for sacred/tender/lyrical; b d g k p t z h for bodily/everyday/harsh; playful b c p for beloved small creatures; related meanings may share a consonant frame; no suffix-look-alike endings (-ti -ri -na -vu -yo -asa); at least two letters from every root and small word except deliberate families. Not retroactive.

A respelled root keeps every meaning and empty slot; all forms, derivations, compounds and image compounds respell with it; compound verbs follow the new first letter; 2.0 spellings retired, 2.0 texts read under 2.0 spellings; overrides protected for these 30 roots; new spellings protected.
volda -> larbopagobudi (larbopago + budi); taha -> kezupago (kezu + pago). Compound reading of kezupago is canon.

rulings_2_2.ruling: A ki-word may open the clause or stay where its answer would stand; the album fronts it in most questions. A yes/no question must end in ki. A question with a ki-word may end in ki or not. Embedded wh-questions may also front the ki-word and never end in ki; embedded yes/no questions use ki-oro (1.0:G2).
examples: maivori ne sabesia ki-coda maivori ramura.

rulings_2_2.ruling: Only ki-modo + adjective, ki-eli + noun and ki-muya + noun make an exclamation, and only when the clause does not end in ki. Any other ki-word clause without ki is a question. A degree question (ki-modo + adjective) must end in ki.
examples: Li nullo ka ki-modo vanisan ki?

rulings_2_2.ruling: tonsi directly before an adjective means “so”; a following fime clause gives the result. Clause-initial tonsi keeps its meaning “therefore”.
examples: taivo ke tonsi corvisan fime taivo viki savalisia maivo ki?
si maivo ke tonsi lukasan, maivo futu ne salrusia.

rulings_2_2.ruling: After a main clause, a fime clause whose verb carries nosi means “in the hope that, so that perhaps”. kopisa stays the plain purpose linker.
examples: maivo futu donuda ito biti de lalfo, fime taivo nosi semnesia ko maivo en moluvaye.

rulings_2_2.ruling: raho with no noun before it means “the one who, that which”, as subject, object or complement. raho is never a question word: questions use ki-nela or ki-coda.
examples: saivo po farufasbifa kube saivo ramura raho maivo po ke.

superseded_in_part.clause: raho is never a question word

rulings_2_2.ruling: An adjective may take sidu + verb for “easy to …, ready to …”. The verb’s object is what the adjective describes.
examples: ito ke ruli levasan sidu zeldoza trana.

rulings_2_2.topic: kroti and krotiapo before a clause
rulings_2_2.ruling: kroti and krotiapo may introduce a clause: “before …”, “after …”. The clause inherits tense like kube (0.8:R6). Before a measure they keep 2.1:G55; before li + noun, their 2.0 meaning.
examples: kroti maivo lesvu taivo ke li sevusan ruhe.

rulings_2_2.ruling: nazru (behind), zavme (in front of), silda (beside), cemnu (in the middle of), lizma (left of) and rizno (right of) may stand bare before a noun phrase as prepositions, or after a verb as adverbs.
examples: Li lavra semnesia nazru li nimu.
saivo de melonulu venreva nazru gase baba lira de ruhesonbu.

rulings_2_2.ruling: The album (twelve songs and the alternate 05) is canon 2.0 text, read with 2.0 spellings under 2.1:G58. A construction it uses consistently is grammar. A line that departs from the grammar once is an album reading: it keeps its intended meaning, is listed with its standard form, and is not a model for new text.

rulings_2_3.ruling: Thirteen roots are respelled: lenra -> zarku; vanru -> dokra; voho -> kezdo; vabale -> tobra; teyo -> dento; mege -> yumli; kupa -> ruko; jemla -> zimzi; pesbi -> bondo; menha -> gamdo; vugo -> vizu; salye -> bapi; senba -> linle. 2.1:G58 applies in full: a respelled root keeps every meaning and empty slot; all forms, derivations, compounds and image compounds respell with it; compound verbs follow the new first letter; 2.2 spellings retired; older texts, including the album, are read under the spellings they were written in.

bumbo (bear), murmu (cow; cattle) and kerku (frog) are new roots. They replace larbopagoregna, maremirulazu and the listed derivation mirunululirayo, which are retired; kerku takes the verb kerkuka, to croak. mirunululira (river-song) stays.
larbopagobudi -> farvibudi (farvi + budi), 'wild dog', read like farvilazu (wild animal); lunolarbopagobudi -> lunofarvibudi. Supersedes the wolf half of 2.1:G59; its taha -> kezupago half stands.
ata may open a line or clause that continues the one before, as oro may (1.2:G25): 'And …'. The album opens lines with ata throughout (2.2:G68).
examples: ata maivo lemula saivo de sizosan lumi.
And I learn his shimmering light.
And we sing again and answer!

rulings_2_3.ruling: en + an abstract noun names the manner or medium of an act: en baba melosan valla, in a musical voice; en veraasa, in truth. ko + a feeling names the spirit in which it is done: ko amor, with love; ko bapi, in surprise. yuta stays the tool or means (1.2:G33); with an abstract noun, choose by meaning. As the album sings (2.2:G68).
examples: saivo po senosia en baba melosan valla.
She spoke in a musical voice.
And the stars wrote in surprise on the strength of phoenix-like love.

rulings_2_3.ruling: A direct question may open with raho for 'who' or 'what' and ends in ki, as the album asks twice (05:22, 11:12). ki-nela and ki-coda remain the ordinary question words. Supersedes the clause of 2.2:G64 that raho is never a question word; headless raho stands.
examples: raho povi sabesia baba kasi polvasan sove ki?
Who can know a more powerful peace?

rulings_2_3.ruling: pagopa (to go) is a motion verb: the motion prefixes attach to it, as in taro-pagopa, to go across (album 05alt). The prefixes stay a closed list, on the motion verbs and the curated metaphors only (1.2:G35).
examples: taivo ne taro-pagopa, nara lalfola hupi li lelde,
you do not go across, but float above the edge,

rulings_2_3.ruling: A question with ki-eli + noun or ki-muya + noun ends in ki; without ki the clause is an exclamation (2.2:G61). Other ki-word questions may still end without ki (2.2:G60).
An embedded yes/no question is opened by ki-oro, never by si, which means only 'if' (1.0:G2, 2.2:G60). Supersedes the clause of 0.8:G4 that has si mean 'whether'.
examples: Maivo masuma ki-oro taivo futu relnura.
I ask whether you will return.

rulings_2_3.ruling: nara may open a line that continues the one before, as ata and oro may (2.3:G72, 1.2:G25). Hortative yava stands where the subject would, opening the clause. A frame may hold more than one time phrase, the wider first. A clause closes in this order: a closing time word, an attitude word, ki (1.2:G24, 1.0:G22).
examples: Nara li devi po ne lenila.
But the goddess did not listen.
Saivori de lira sasvasia taivo toda-krono pifu.
May their song protect you always.

amended_by.scope: 2.3:G78 (closing order only; its other clauses stand)

rulings_2_3.ruling: A measure is a number or a quantifier with a unit: kroti + a measure is 'ago' (kroti dossa deya, two days ago), and kroti + a bare noun is 'before' it (kroti deya) (2.1:G55). 'Since' a time is da + the time word: da ola-krono, since then. tuni may take a noun phrase of time: tuni merno, until morning.
examples: Maivo po venreva kroti dossa deya.
Since then, we sing to each other.
Li lirayo po sulnosia tuni merno.

rulings_2_3.ruling: 1.2:G30 extends to verbs of hearing, knowing and thinking: give the verb an object with a de phrase. Saivo po lenila li telne de li lirayo, he heard about the singer (the story of the singer).
examples: Li tarnuregna po lenila li telne de li lirayo.
The king heard about the singer.

rulings_2_3.ruling: Before a number or quantity, lusu and mosa are 'at least' and 'at most' (1.0:G9); before an adjective they make the superlative: mosa vanisan, most beautiful; lusu vanisan, least beautiful.
examples: Taivo guraga maivo lusu dossa cono.
You owe me at least two coins.
Taivo de lira ka mosa vanisan.
Your song is the most beautiful.

rulings_2_3.topic: An adjective noun keeps its article
rulings_2_3.ruling: An adjective standing as a noun keeps its determiner even where li could otherwise be omitted (0.8:R5, 1.2:G29): li corvisan, the brave one.

A direct quotation follows its verb of saying after a colon, in quotation marks; ki may close the main clause before it (0.8:G4). An exclamation in the past uses ki-modo + adjective with a copula and its tense (2.2:G61).
examples: Li devi po masuma: “Ki-nela roni lirala ki?”
Li nullo po ka ki-modo vanisan!

rulings_2_3.ruling: A superseded ruling is kept as it was ruled. A construction it allowed stays grammatical in texts written under it and is not wrong in new text, but the superseding ruling is the one to follow.

A listed derivation retired for a headword stays buildable with its default reading (2.0:G41); a text written before the retirement reads it through the legacy table, as mirunululirayo reads kerku (2.3:G70).
Whether an ascended form (-asa, -asasan) is sacred or simply the highest degree of its root depends on the word and its gloss; a sacred text uses the sacred ones (0.8:R10).

rulings_2_5.topic: The album is not grammar canon
rulings_2_5.ruling: The album 'Liraasa: Songs of the First Stars' is not grammar canon. It stays in the data as text, marked non-normative. No album line licenses a construction, and album_reading annotations no longer grant exceptions.

rulings_2_5.topic: Questions end in ki; a fronted ki-word may drop it
rulings_2_5.ruling: A yes/no question ends in ki. A content question ends in ki unless its ki-word is the first word of the sentence; a ki-word left in its answer's place requires the final ki. This exception covers ki-coda, ki-pago, ki-krono, ki-nela, ki-nela de, ki-kasa, manner ki-modo and ki-muya-krono only. Questions with ki-eli + noun, ki-muya + noun and degree ki-modo + adjective always end in ki (2.3:G76, 2.2:G61 stand), and the same three without ki remain exclamations. Embedded questions never take ki (2.3:G77 stands). A ki-word in its answer's place in a clause without final ki is an embedded question or part of a statement, never a direct question.
examples: Ki-kasa taivo po amora maivo ki?
Maivo po masuma li talirivo ki-kasa.
examples_ungrammatical: ki-word in place without final ki is not a question
ki-eli + noun questions always end in ki
rulings_2_5.notes: This also resolves I-02 (three live statements of the question rule).

rulings_2_5.topic: Which clause a final ki or attitude word belongs to
rulings_2_5.ruling: A ki or attitude word (seye, mufe, poye, pifu, zoke) at the end of a sentence belongs to the main clause, even when a subordinate clause follows it. Doubt inside a trailing subordinate clause is expressed with a modal (nosi); an embedded yes/no question uses ki-oro. ki is the last word of the sentence, except that a vocative set off by a comma may follow it.
examples: Taivo sabesia fime maivo lirala poye.
Perhaps you know that I sing.
Taivo sabesia fime maivo nosi lirala.
You know that I might sing.
Taivo sabesia fime maivo lirala ki?
Do you know that I sing?
rulings_2_5.notes: 0.8:G4 (ki may also close the main clause before an appended direct quotation) stands.

rulings_2_5.topic: The clause's closing order and its edge positions
rulings_2_5.ruling: A clause closes in this order: … VERB [OBJECT] [ADJUNCTS] [fuyi] [STATUS: hoyo | yasmo] [ATTITUDE] [ki]. Closing time words, durations and clause-final reve / loki stand among the adjuncts, before fuyi. Outside the core slots, a clause has edge positions. Before it, in order: a line linker (ata, oro, nara), FRAME, TOPIC, then a fronted ki-word (2.5:G88). After it: a vocative set off by a comma, which may follow ki.
examples: May we always sing to each other.
Taivo viki pagopa ligo maivo ki, maivo de amor?
Would you come near me, my love?
amends: 2.3:G78 (closing order only; its other clauses stand)
derived: The edge positions (line linker, FRAME, TOPIC, fronted ki-word; vocative after the clause) were part of the lean, not option A itself. They are needed to make 2.5:G88 and the existing line-initial ata / vocative rulings fit the template. Confirm.
Durations and clause-final reve / loki sit among the adjuncts, like closing time words. Confirm.
rulings_2_5.notes: This also resolves I-03 (constructions the rulings allow but the template had no slot for).

rulings_2_5.ruling: FRAME, the clause-opening slot set off by a comma, holds a time adverbial or a place adverbial. Tense words (po, futu, pressa) and iteration words (reve, loki, bodu) are not frame words and are never closing time words.
examples_ungrammatical: po is a tense word, not a closing time word
derived: 'Place adverbial' covers place correlatives (eli-pago, ola-pago, toda-pago …) and prepositional phrases of place (En li nimu, …). Confirm.

rulings_2_5.ruling: A command is marked. In writing it ends in '!' or contains fisa; in speech, fisa or command intonation marks it. A subjectless, tenseless clause with neither mark is an elliptical statement, not a command.
derived: In speech, command intonation stands in for the written '!'. Confirm.
rulings_2_5.notes: I-42 (which operators a command may carry; yava's position with a FRAME) was not decided. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings_2_5.ruling: A fragment question follows the ki rule: it ends in ki.
Echo ki attaches only to a single word or a bare noun phrase. raho + clause + ki is therefore always a direct question (2.3:G74 stands).

rulings_2_5.topic: ke and ka: one contrast for every predicate
rulings_2_5.ruling: ke and ka mark one contrast for every kind of predicate (adjective, noun phrase or location): ke = holds now, or for a time; ka = lasting, defining, by nature.
supersedes: clause.copulas definitions of ke and ka
examples: Li kavbikova ke su li tabu.
The basket is on the table (right now).
Li nimu ka ligo li cilni.
The home is near the city (it always has been).
I was a little child (back then).
I am a singer (it's who I am).
The person is good at the moment.
The friend is good by nature.

rulings_2_5.ruling: The minimal clause is SUBJECT + VERB, with these exceptions: commands, hortatives, permitted ellipsis, existential miyo clauses (which have no subject), and bare adjective predicates. A bare adjective predicate (SUBJECT ADJECTIVE, no copula) is allowed only in the present with no operators; anything more needs ke or ka.
examples: Miyo baba sora en li nimu.
There is a friend in the home.
examples_ungrammatical: a bare adjective predicate takes no operators
a bare adjective predicate takes no operators
rulings_2_5.notes: A bare predicate carries no ke / ka contrast (2.5:G93); use a copula when that contrast matters.

rulings_2_5.ruling: po ka = was (lasting), with no claim about now. kapoki = was, and no longer is. (With 2.5:G93, po ke = was, at that time.)
examples: They were good (no claim about now).
They were good, and no longer are.

rulings_2_5.topic: Kinship nouns are not names for possession
rulings_2_5.ruling: Kinship nouns (pilo, mare and the rest) are never treated as names for possession. Only a pronoun, or a personal name standing before de, is the owner; otherwise X de Y = 'X of Y' (Y owns). When both sides are personal names, the left one owns.
derived: Two names: the left one owns. The author chose C; this follows from 1.2:G27 (a name before de owns) and is listed for confirmation.

rulings_2_5.ruling: Chains of de group from the left: X de Y de Z = (X de Y) de Z. The ownership rules apply first to X de Y, then to that whole phrase de Z.
examples: li suma de maivo de yuge
my warmth, of the body  [(li suma de maivo) de yuge]
rulings_2_5.translator_preference: When the intended meaning groups from the right ('the warmth of my body'), do not produce a three-part chain. Rephrase, for example with an adjective form or a second sentence.

rulings_2_5.ruling: NUMBER de NUMBER may be a fraction or a partitive; context decides. Fractions are written with spaces (tressa de cuara), never hyphenated.
examples: One of the two will return / One half will return.
rulings_2_5.translator_preference: For a partitive, prefer an article (una de li dossa) so the output is not ambiguous.

rulings_2_5.ruling: Noun-phrase order: [QUANTIFIER] [DETERMINER: li | baba | eli | ola | eliri | olari | ki-eli | OWNER de] [ORDINAL] [NUMBER] {[DEGREE WORD] ADJECTIVE} NOUN[-ti][-ri] [de NP] [raho CLAUSE]. The ordinal stands right after the determiner, before the adjectives. Degree words (ruli, kasi, menu, mosa, lusu, gase, diba) stand directly before the adjective they modify. ki-muya fills the QUANTIFIER slot. OWNER de takes only a pronoun or a personal name (2.5:G95).
derived: ORDINAL before NUMBER (li una-ne dossa lirari, 'the first two songs'), following English order. Confirm.
rulings_2_5.notes: The order of two or more adjectives (A4.22) is still undecided. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings_2_5.ruling: li may not be dropped after a side noun (nazru, zavme, silda, cemnu, lizma, rizno) used as a preposition.
examples: Li lavra semnesia nazru li nimu.
The bird sits behind the home.
examples_ungrammatical: li dropped after a side noun

rulings_2_5.ruling: maivo is deliberately both the pronoun 'I' and the noun 'Self'. Context decides.
examples: I am beautiful. / The Self is beautiful.
rulings_2_5.translator_preference: Always write the noun as li maivo, so translator output is never ambiguous.

rulings_2_5.topic: Which words take -ri, and plural agreement
rulings_2_5.ruling: -ri attaches to nouns, pronouns, demonstratives, and an adjective used as a noun after a determiner; never to a bare adjective or a verb. After any count word (a number, a quantifier, eliri or olari), -ri on the noun is optional, chosen by sound and meter. A singular demonstrative (eli, ola) takes a singular noun.
examples_ungrammatical: singular demonstrative with a plural noun
derived: 'A singular demonstrative takes a singular noun' makes the ✗ example of option B explicit. Confirm.

rulings_2_5.ruling: An animal is referred to with ito by default. A named animal takes saivo.
examples: Li lavra lirala; ito ka vanisan.
The bird sings; it is beautiful.
Nilo (the bird) sings; she is beautiful.
rulings_2_5.notes: sela (reflexive only, or also emphatic) and whether maivori includes the listener were not decided. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings_2_5.ruling: Only listed time adverbials stand bare as 'when': entries in the time-adverbial table, -krono correlatives, and day compounds (deyapressa, deyaapo, deyafutu). A plain time noun (merno, nullo, vesno, mambi, lornu …) used as 'when' takes en. A bare plain noun after a verb is its object.
rulings_2_5.notes: Duration ('for two days', 2.1:G55 bare measure after the object) still collides with an object reading. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings_2_5.topic: yuta, en, ko and la: one test per word
rulings_2_5.ruling: One test per word. yuta = a tool, means or substance handled or used up. en = a medium or state one is in, including a manner seen as a medium. ko = a companion, or an emotion that accompanies the act. la + adjective = the quality of the action.
examples: Maivo lallela li dorbi yuta li kemye.
I open the door with the key.
Saivo po senosia en baba melosan valla.
She spoke in a musical voice.
rulings_2_5.notes: The en/intra and transa/taro- overlaps named in I-25 were not decided.

rulings_2_5.ruling: la + adjective stands only among the adjuncts, after the verb and object. A degree word goes between la and the adjective: la ruli molusan.
Amounts: kasi or menu + noun … tamo NP. Manner: la kasi (or la menu) + adjective … tamo NP.
examples: Maivo tovota kasi lirari tamo taivo.
I have more songs than you.
Maivo lirala la kasi molusan tamo taivo.
I sing more gently than you.
examples_ungrammatical: bare kasi after the verb is not licensed (option B was not chosen)
rulings_2_5.notes: Comparing an action with no manner adjective ('I sing more than you', 'I love you more than …') still has no form. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings_2_5.ruling: gase + a number may mean 'about' or 'like'; context decides.
examples: I have about two coins. / … something like two coins.
rulings_2_5.translator_preference: For 'about N' write gase N; for a simile write gase li N (with the article), so output is unambiguous.

rulings_2_5.ruling: A measure (for kroti 'ago' and krotiapo 'from now') is NUMBER + unit, or a listed quantifier + unit. Listed quantifiers: AUTHOR INPUT NEEDED.
examples: Maivo po venreva kroti dossa deya.
rulings_2_5.notes: Do not invent the list. Until the author supplies it, treat only NUMBER + unit as a measure and report kroti + quantifier + noun as unresolved.

rulings_2_5.ruling: Valency operators vaku (make), lesvu (let) and tekvu (prevent): CAUSER [TENSE] [noma] [ne] [MODAL] … [EVIDENTIAL] OP ACTOR [ne] [APPROACH] [PHASE] [EFFORT] VERB [OBJECT]. Tense, modal and evidential belong to the main clause; the actor's own negation, approach, phase and effort follow the actor. The embedded verb may take an object.
examples: Maivo vaku saivo sapusia li nami.
I make him eat the food.

rulings_2_5.ruling: gome may passivise any verb that is attested with an object anywhere in the data. Without gome, the subject is the doer, except for the listed change-of-state verbs, whose subject may be the thing that changes (an anticausative reading).
examples: Li lira gome sarbisia gagu maivo.
The song is written by me.
Zafra, li dorbi po gome lallela.

rulings_2_5.topic: Adjective + sidu + verb: no dummy ito
rulings_2_5.ruling: In ADJECTIVE + sidu + VERB, the thing the adjective describes is the subject of the clause and the understood object of the verb. There is no dummy ito.
examples: Trana ke ruli levasan sidu zeldoza.
Change is very easy to resist.
examples_ungrammatical: Ito ke ruli levasan sidu zeldoza trana.
dummy ito with an overt object

rulings_2_5.ruling: A pronoun recipient may stand bare right after any verb whose meaning has a recipient (giving, lending, sending, owing, paying, bringing, teaching, showing, telling, singing to …). Otherwise, and always for a non-pronoun recipient, the recipient takes ala after the theme.
examples: Maivo lirala baba lira ala taivo.
I sing a song to you.

rulings_2_5.ruling: Purpose always uses kopisa. With the same subject, kopisa + bare verb phrase (no subject); with a different subject, kopisa + clause. sidu stays for verb chains (desida sidu lirala).
examples: Maivo po venreva eli-pago kopisa lirala.
I sing so that you dance.
examples_ungrammatical: Maivo po venreva eli-pago sidu lirala.
sidu is not used for purpose
rulings_2_5.notes: ke sidu ('destined to', open_questions_do_not_resolve[3]) stays open.

rulings_2_5.ruling: 'Would have' is always po noma viki. po viki without noma is not a form.
examples: Si maivo po noma masuma, taivo po noma viki relsira.
If I had asked, you would have answered.

rulings_2_5.topic: The comma that closes a raho clause
rulings_2_5.ruling: A raho clause that does not end the sentence is closed by a comma (a pause in speech) when it contains its own object or adjunct. A raho clause of only a verb (and its operators) needs no comma.
examples: Li nela raho lirala ka benasan.
The person who sings is good.
Li sabeyo raho vismava eli, ne yehu vimova li vordu.
The sage who studies this did not witness the word.
examples_ungrammatical: Li sabeyo raho vismava eli ne yehu vimova li vordu.
relative clause with an object, not closed by a comma

rulings_2_5.ruling: Hopeful purpose ('so that perhaps', 'in the hope that') is kopisa + a clause whose verb carries nosi. fime always introduces a content clause ('that').
examples: Maivo lirala, kopisa taivo nosi rilura.
I sing, so that perhaps you'll dance.
Maivo sabesia fime taivo nosi lirala.
I know that you might sing.

rulings_2_5.ruling: Clause-initial tonsi means 'therefore' and is followed by a comma. tonsi meaning 'so' (degree) stands only before a predicate adjective, after a copula.
examples: Taivo ke tonsi corvisan fime taivo viki savalisia maivo ki?
Are you so brave that you would kiss me?

rulings_2_5.ruling: An unmarked subordinate clause takes the main clause's tense, whatever its linker. sige clauses are the exception and always mark their own tense. A subordinate clause with its own tense word keeps it.
examples: Kureli taivo venreva, maivo po lirala.
As soon as you came, I sang.
Maivo po masuma ki-oro taivo relnura.
settles_open_questions: open_questions_do_not_resolve[5] (tense after kureli, sina, si, nevi)
rulings_2_5.notes: Clauses opened by clause adverbs (tonsi, narli, korsi, krotiata) and coordinated ata / nara clauses are main clauses, not subordinate, and are outside this rule.

rulings_2_5.ruling: A topic that is the subject of its clause must be picked up by a pronoun. A non-subject topic may be picked up or left as a gap; a gap is read as the verb's object.
examples: Li bumre hozi, Kipo po bumreba.
As for the bread, Kipo baked it.
Li bumre hozi, Kipo po bumreba ito.
As for the bread, Kipo baked it.
derived: 'A gap is read as the verb's object' resolves the remaining ambiguity of option C. Confirm.

rulings_2_5.topic: Relatives on a possessor, a time or a place
rulings_2_5.ruling: Relative clauses on a possessor, a time or a place use a resumptive pronoun in place, as 2.1:G52 does for prepositions: possessor → PRONOUN de NOUN; time or place → the needed preposition + ito.
examples: li lirayo raho maivo amora saivo de lira
the singer whose song I love
li krono raho maivo po lirala en ito
li pago raho maivo po venreva da ito

rulings_2_5.ruling: The motion prefixes are productive on any verb, with compositional meanings: va- = toward the speaker, here; du- = away, giving away; taro- = across, through; yave- = together, to meet; revo- = back, again. A listed meaning (the four curated phrases and any listed prefixed verb) overrides the compositional one. 'Motion verb' is no longer a category the grammar needs. lu-, nu-, mi-, so- stay retired.
rulings_2_5.notes: This also resolves I-06 (the undefined class of motion verbs).

rulings_2_5.ruling: -ti is an inflection-like suffix, not one of the derivations. Word ::= ROOT + (one form OR one derivation) + -ti + -ri; -ti may follow any form or derivation.
A word ending in pago is the same word whether read as ROOT + -pago or as a compound with the root pago. It is a noun with no further forms unless its dictionary line lists them.

rulings_2_5.topic: Image compounds have all seven forms
rulings_2_5.ruling: Image compounds have all seven forms, built by the ordinary form rules, with predictable meanings. This is an explicit exception to hard_rules[1] ('only listed forms exist'), which still governs every other headword.
derived: Proposed meaning templates, for confirmation: noun = the image; -asa = the image at its highest or sacred degree; -na = the absence or opposite of the image; verb = to make, do or bring about the image; -san = having the quality of the image; -asasan = supremely so; -nasan = lacking the image.
rulings_2_5.translator_preference: Prefer attested image compounds and their attested readings; use a predicted form only when no listed word fits, and flag it in the output.

rulings_2_5.ruling: Negative numbers: antizi + NUMBER (antizi dossa = minus two). antizi is a new function word.
rulings_2_5.notes: Decimals were not decided and remain outside the language.

rulings_3_0.ruling: iya + noun phrase is a vocative: a direct address. It opens a sentence and is set off by a comma, stands alone as an invocation, or follows a final ki after a comma (2.5:G89). The noun phrase may be a name, a title, an epithet, a pronoun (taivo, taivori) or an owned phrase (maivo de amor). A vocative never changes the grammar of the clause it addresses. In everyday speech a bare name set off by commas remains a vocative (1.2:G31); in prayer, invocation and litany iya is expected, and it is required wherever a comma-set noun phrase could be read as an apposition (3.0:G130).
examples: Iya li mare de li lumi, maivo lirala vobi taivo.
O mother of light, I sing for you.
Taivo viki pagopa ligo maivo ki, iya maivo de amor?
Would you come near me, O my love?
examples_ungrammatical: iya is not followed by a comma: it belongs to its noun phrase
rulings_3_0.notes: The hymn and every prayer genre address the divine; 2.5 had no vocative particle (open question).

rulings_3_0.ruling: A noun phrase may be followed by a second noun phrase, set off by commas, that renames it: an apposition. The apposed phrase keeps its own determiner, takes no copula, and is closed by a comma when the clause continues. Each phrase settles its own de-ownership: an apposition starts a new phrase, so it never joins a de-chain (2.5:G96). Several appositions in a row form a litany. A relative clause (raho) may end an apposition.
examples: Li mareasa de li vemiasa, li una-ne lumi raho po kronobioka li veluri, po ke lavisan.
The mother of the cosmos, the first light who gave birth to the stars, was glad.
Deviasa, li mare de li veluri, lirala.
The Great Goddess, the mother of the stars, sings.
li lumi, li lumi de li veluri
the light, the light of the stars
O Great Goddess, Mother of the Stars, Mother of Light, Mother of Song!
examples_ungrammatical: Deviasa li mare de li veluri lirala.
an apposition must be set off by commas
rulings_3_0.notes: Hymn line 11 (‘The cosmic mother, the first light who birthed stars, was pleased …’) had to be split into two statements; epithets and litanies depend on apposition.

rulings_3_0.ruling: An ascended noun or title compound used as a name of the Goddess is capitalized and takes no article (Deviasa, Lumiasa, Mareasa, Velumare). Used as a name, it owns like a personal name when it stands before de (1.2:G27): Deviasa de lira is the Great Goddess’s song. An epithet that describes her keeps its article and stays lower-case: li mare de li lumi, the mother of light. Writing a descriptive epithet as a name therefore changes its meaning.
examples: the Great Goddess’s song (a name owns)
the mother of light (an epithet: the light ‘owns’ the relation)
examples_ungrammatical: Mareasa de li lumi (meaning ‘the mother of light’)
as a name, Mareasa owns: this reads ‘the Mother’s light’; write li mareasa de li lumi
rulings_3_0.notes: Titles are central to devotion, but 2.5 lets a name before de own; a capitalized ‘Mareasa de li lumi’ would silently mean ‘the Mother’s light’.

rulings_3_0.ruling: miyo with a subject before it and no noun phrase after it asserts that the subject exists: absolute being. It takes tense, negation and operators like any verb. miyo + noun phrase with no subject keeps its 2.5 meaning, ‘there is’. A copula (ke, ka) still always needs a predicate.
examples: Saivo po miyo, saivo miyo, saivo futu miyo.
She was, she is, she will be.
Kroti li pagoasa, Deviasa po miyo.
Before the universe, the Great Goddess was.
Miyo baba sora en li nimu.
There is a friend in the home. (2.5 meaning, unchanged)
examples_ungrammatical: a copula needs a predicate; use Saivo po miyo
rulings_3_0.notes: ‘She was, she is, she will be’ and ‘I am’ could not be said in 2.5; sacred languages need a statement of existence by itself.

rulings_3_0.topic: Fiat, blessing of existence, and the liturgical formulas
rulings_3_0.ruling: miyo + noun phrase marked as a command (‘!’) is a fiat: ‘let there be …’. miyo + noun phrase + pifu is a wish: ‘may there be …’. Unmarked, miyo + noun phrase stays a statement (2.5:G90). Two fixed liturgical formulas are canon: ‘Ola-modo po miyo, ola-modo miyo, ola-modo futu miyo’ (so it was, so it is, so it shall be), in which ola-modo opens an existential clause without a comma; and ‘Ola-modo pifu’ (so be it; amen), which closes a prayer.
examples: Miyo sove en li nimu pifu.
May there be peace in the home.
Ola-modo po miyo, ola-modo miyo, ola-modo futu miyo.
So it was, so it is, so it shall be.
examples_ungrammatical: Ola po ka, ola ka, ola futu ka.
rulings_3_0.notes: Hymn line 23 had to become ‘that was true, is true, will be true’; creation myths need ‘let there be’.

rulings_3_0.ruling: A pronoun or noun phrase + sela in subject position, or as an apposition, is emphatic: ‘herself’, ‘itself’. In object position, PRONOUN sela stays reflexive (unchanged). sela never stands alone as a subject.
examples: Ito sela po ka li una-ne leninela.
It itself was the first listener.
Saivo de nole po ka sambasan ko li melo, ito sela.
Her name was the same as music, music itself.
examples_ungrammatical: sela needs a pronoun or noun phrase before it
settles_open_questions: sela: reflexive object only, or also emphatic (the maivori half stays open).
rulings_3_0.notes: Hymn lines 8 and 17 (‘was itself the first’, ‘music itself’) could not carry the emphasis.

rulings_3_0.ruling: A command may carry ne, the iteration words reve and loki, and any adjuncts; it never carries tense, a modal or an evidential. A petition to the divine is a command opened by a vocative (3.0:G129), usually softened by fisa after the vocative’s comma. yava may follow a FRAME.
examples: Iya Deviasa, fisa, ne pagopa vofa maivo!
O Great Goddess, please, do not go far from me!
Iya Lumimare, fisa, lenila maivo de lirajuba.
O Mother of Light, please hear my song-offering.
settles_open_questions: Which operators a command may carry, and whether yava stands after a FRAME or always first.
rulings_3_0.notes: Prayer is built on petitions; 2.5 left open which operators a command may carry and where yava may stand.

rulings_3_0.ruling: After a noun naming a made work (lira, lavbulira, lirasarbi, telne, sarbiasa …), gagu + noun phrase names its maker, without a passive verb. Elsewhere gagu remains the agent of gome (2.5:G110).
examples: Liraasa, li lira de li una-ne veluri gagu li una-ne mareasa
Liraasa, the song of the first stars, by the first mother
examples_ungrammatical: gagu follows the work, never precedes it
rulings_3_0.notes: Hymn line 24 (‘by the first mother’) had to use da, ‘from’.

rulings_3_0.ruling: A verbless acclamation NP ala NP! (‘NP to NP!’) is grammatical as a liturgical fragment: glory, praise or thanks offered to someone. It may be followed by a vocative.
examples: Praise to you, O Mother of Light!
Thanks to you, O Mother of the Stars.
rulings_3_0.notes: Doxologies and praise lines (‘Glory to …’) had no form.

rulings_3_0.ruling: Taivo, Saivo and their forms may be capitalized mid-sentence when they refer to the Goddess. This is an optional convention of written devotion and has no grammatical effect.
examples: Saivo miyo, ata Saivo de lumi lumila.
She is, and Her light shines.

rulings_3_0.ruling: The new noun rinbakrono (eternity) is a time noun: as ‘when’ it takes en (2.5:G103). en rinbakrono means ‘for ever; in eternity’. toda-krono (always) is unchanged. Durations in general (‘for two days’) remain an open question.

A bare noun or number repeated around krotiapo (‘X after X’) is a distributive adjunct or FRAME meaning ‘one X after another’: una krotiapo una, one by one; velu krotiapo velu, star after star. It extends kroti/krotiapo + a bare noun (2.3:G79).
examples: Una krotiapo una, li veluri po hiro lirala.
One by one, the stars began to sing.
Velu krotiapo velu, li navu po loya lumisan.
Star after star, the sky became bright.
rulings_3_0.notes: Hymn line 12 (‘One by one, star by star’) had no form.

rulings_3_0.ruling: Ascended forms are most powerful against ordinary ones. Keep ordinary forms for the human and the near; reserve ascended forms for what is truly divine; let a change of register mark a change of nearness (a mortal growing toward the divine, or the Goddess stooping to comfort). This is guidance for composition, not grammar.
examples: Maivo ke nemesan. Taivo ka loreasa.
I am sorrowful. You are a heart larger than sorrow.

rulings_3_2.ruling: A small set of archetype modifiers combines with archetype heads to name kinds of a thing. Modifiers: gudo (common, ordinary), zile (fine, fancy), farvi (wild), yalmu (powered), krono (aged), and any time or place noun. Heads: pocu (fowl), kadu (vehicle), kaze (gun), velma (clothing), nami (food), miru (infused drink), favro (signal device), bujo (joint), nela (person). A pair is read 'the MODIFIER sort of HEAD', but its listed meaning is binding and specific: gudopocu is chicken, not any common bird. Unlisted pairs may be coined by rule and must be flagged until listed. -vu (big) and -ti (small) apply as usual: pocuvu turkey, pocuti chick.
In eating and cooking, an animal noun also names its meat, as English chicken and fish do: sapusia gudopocu, to eat chicken. yugenami (meat) remains the general word; X de yugenami is never needed.

Body-part nouns double as units of length when they follow a number: pebu (a foot), fini (a finger-width, roughly an inch), varo (an arm-length, roughly a yard). valmilornu (an hour's walk) is the long unit. cono (coin) is the generic money unit.

zilenela placed directly before a name, with no comma, is an honorific title: Mr, Mrs, Ms. As a vocative, iya zilenela is sir or madam. A kinship or rank word may stand before a name the same way (pilo Peta, Father Peta).

Further archetype heads under 3.2:G142: furo (fruit; a colour base names the fruit: rubifuro apple, aurumifuro lemon, viofuroti grape), herba (plant, vegetable), marna (grain), pusa (powder), nami (dish), kova (container), biti (tool), velma (garment), rinba (ring, jewelry), zupa (room), domlu (building). Listed meanings are binding; unlisted pairs are flagged.
A copied place name (2.0:G45) + -san is an adjective of origin: Fransa + -san = Fransasan, French. The bare name stays a noun; de + the name means from the place.

rulings_3_3.topic: Relational adjectives from compounds and derivations
rulings_3_3.ruling: The adjective slot (-san) of any compound, listed derivation or image compound is available by rule, with the reading 'of, relating to, or marked by X', unless the lexicon lists another meaning for it. For roots, only listed forms exist (unchanged). This supplies English relational adjectives (theological, railway, comic, muddy, distant) without listing each one.

Placeholder [sure] replaced with the canonical certainty marker seye.

rulings_0_8.ruling: The JSON is authoritative; the workbook is generated. Language field and files are named Liraasa.
An unused form may receive a gloss only when its compositional meaning is predictable, approved case by case, and recorded in authorized_changes.
Frozen for 0.8. No canonical root is respelled; the 40-root queue carries forward unchanged.

A standalone tense particle opening a paragraph or turn (Po — / Futu —) sets a frame: following unmarked main clauses take that tense until another tense particle, pressa, or the end of the paragraph. Optional. Time words do not set a frame, so 0.7 texts keep their meaning.
li may be omitted in everyday speech as well as verse when the referent is obvious; never when ambiguous. baba may be omitted only in verse.
sige clauses never inherit tense; they are always marked. Tense inheritance applies to fime, raho, kube, nayo, kasa, kopisa and tuni.
deyaapo is kept as a fossil (it retains the retired past marker apo). apo is not used in new compounds; say vesno de deyaapo.
amorliraa, amorrinbaa and amorvulraa are correct; each a is its own syllable.
A certainty marker (or zoke) precedes ki: Taivo lirala poye ki?
Registers are defined in the grammar guide. The lexicon keeps everyday and poetic labels; sacred is added only to headwords whose root meaning is inherently sacred, after review.
New vocabulary is sized by genuine gaps, not by the 120-150 target.
The diminutive -ti may attach to personal names as an affectionate or teasing form (Dorinti).

eli/ola (and eliri/olari) stand alone for things, situations and discourse (ola = what was just said; eli = what follows). For people use eli-nela/ola-nela or saivo, except presentational Eli ka NAME.

ne precedes what it negates: verb or modal (after tense), copula (ne ka), noun phrase or fragment (Ne eli), or a contrasted constituent (ne X, nara Y). Negation is compositional: ne + nuna- is a positive (avoid).

Everyday speech may omit a repeated subject in coordinated clauses and in answers, omit a repeated predicate after a contrasting subject (Dorin, ne.), answer with tense + verb (Po sapusia.), and echo a word with ki. Speech may break off after any particle; the listener may complete it.

ki may close the main clause before an appended direct quotation (Taivo vurlova ki, fime maivo senosia: "...") as well as after it (0.7 order). Embedded wh-questions keep the wh-word in place with no ki; embedded yes/no questions use si (whether).
Inside an inheriting clause: tefa marks prior action, nayo/roni simultaneous, futu subsequent (future-in-past), sahi habitual.

The root (form 1) is the noun of action or thing (juba, donu, tali). A verb phrase becomes a noun phrase with sidu (Sidu lisrola ka livna de taivo) or a clause with fime (Fime taivo po relnura ka baba juba).
[toda|rada|muya|poka|somi|nuna] [li|eli|ola|OWNER de] [NUMBER] [ADJ...] NOUN[-ti][-ri] [de ...] [raho ...]. toda N = every N; toda li N = all the N; toda OWNER de N = all OWNER's N.
X ka sambasan ko Y (same as); X ka sambanasan da Y (different from); gase NP alone = like NP (simile); gase ADJ gase NP = as ADJ as NP. Lotero silda, ... = on the other hand.

reserved_root_bank.note: Short two-syllable roots (consonant-vowel-consonant-vowel) that still fit every rule: at least two edits from every active word in 1.2 plus this patch, and from each other. The most singable root shape is nearly full, so spend these deliberately: on frequent concepts whose words are long. Unassigned; not part of the language until you give one a meaning. Checked against every Liraasa word in the 1.2 file (headwords, forms, small words, numbers, colours, example sentences) and in this patch. Roots with c are left out because its pronunciation is not fixed in the sound section.

changesets_1_2.summary: Grammar rulings G24–G31 from the open-questions review of 2026-10-17 (ADR-0012), and the three examples ADR-0011 left to revise. 1.1 stays vocabulary-only (ADR-0009); these land on top of it.

The 1.2 lexicon update (ADR-0013): rulings G32–G36, 57 primal roots, 22 compounds, 2 function words, 3 frequency correlatives, 24 lexicalised derivations, 2 curated motion metaphors, 3 reglosses, 6 predictable slots activated, and the protected-exceptions label repaired. Applied after 2026-10-17-grammar-rulings by npm run integrate:1.2.

changesets_2_0.summary: Liraasa 2.0 (ADR-0016), from the author's patch "Liraasa 2.0: the great lexicon expansion": rulings 2.0:G37–G42 (word-building only; no clause, order or inflection rule changes), 10 roots and 346 compounds, 276 slots activated, 207 glosses edited, 77 lexicalised derivations, 391 template headwords moved into the image-compound pattern.

The 2.0 grammar-guide review (ADR-0016 addendum): rulings 2.0:G43 (consonant values), G44 (neighbouring vowels in song) and G45 (foreign names), from the author's answers of 2026-10-18; lumiasa reglossed "Divine Light, Goddess", then "Her Divine Light"; two gloss typos fixed. No grammar rule changes.

changesets_2_1.summary: Liraasa 2.1 (ADR-0017), from the author's patch "Liraasa 2.1": rulings 2.1:G46–G59 (questions in place, exclamatives, blessings, N times, different-subject complements, evidentials, relatives on a prepositional object, partitive de, result clauses, duration, prohibitions, sound follows meaning, respelling); 28 roots respelled and 2 replaced by compounds, with every form, compound, image compound and derivation built on them; the lexicon's fronted questions rewritten under 2.1:G46.

The 2.1 integration review (ADR-0017 addendum), from the author's answers of 2026-10-19: the miyo and loya examples, whose sola now means sun, are deleted; the elliptical question Ata taivo? ends in ki. The new spellings are kept as the patch describes, and kezupagolelde stands. No rule changes.

changesets_2_2.summary: Liraasa 2.2 added rulings 2.2:G60–G68, restored the 2.0 spelling silro (reverting the 2.1 respelling puzu), filled the forms soloasa and tarnulinusan, and added the album as the reference corpus with sixteen album readings.

changesets_2_3.summary: Liraasa 2.3 (ADR-0019), from the author's sound-pass patch: rulings 2.3:G69–G71; 13 roots respelled (lenra → zarku, vanru → dokra, voho → kezdo, vabale → tobra, teyo → dento, mege → yumli, kupa → ruko, jemla → zimzi, pesbi → bondo, menha → gamdo, vugo → vizu, salye → bapi, senba → linle); bear and cow made the roots bumbo and murmu, and frog the new root kerku (mirunululirayo retired); wolf rebuilt as farvibudi (farvi + budi), superseding the wolf half of 2.1:G59; every form, compound, image compound, derivation and example sentence built on them follows.

The 2.3 integration review (ADR-0019 addendum), from the author's answers of 2026-10-19: dento (tooth) and ruko (blood) are kept as the patch substitutes them; the respelled example of 1.2:G28 is kept and its 2.2 text retired to the new archive, legacy.archived_text; the stale history in the notes of bumbo, murmu and mirunululira moves there too; the root bank is left as it is. No rule changes.

The grammar audit's decisions (review/audit-report.md, ADR-0019 addendum), from the author's answers of 2026-10-19. The album's consistent usage becomes grammar: 2.3:G72 (line-initial ata), G73 (manner with en and ko), G74 (raho opening a question, superseding that clause of 2.2:G64) and G75 (pagopa takes the motion prefixes). Left to the editor's judgement: G76 (ki-eli and ki-muya questions end in ki), G77 (si is never 'whether', superseding that clause of 0.8:G4), G78 (opening and closing a clause), G79 (time phrases), G80 ('about' after hearing and knowing), G81 (lusu and mosa), G82 (an adjective noun keeps li), G83 (quotations, past exclamations), G84 (superseded rulings) and G85 (retired listed derivations). G86: whether an ascended form is sacred depends on the word. Tense inheritance after kureli, sina, si and nevi stays open. Stale texts in morphology and the numbers table corrected; a function-word example and a note cleaned.

changesets_2_5.summary: Liraasa 2.5, step 1 (D-00): 2.5:G87 retires the album as grammar canon, superseding 2.2:G68. The album stays as text, marked non-normative; its readings grant no exceptions. From the author's 2.5 patch (data/proposals/liraasa_2_5_patch.json).

Liraasa 2.5, step 2: the author's decisions on the 2.3 grammar audit (review/grammar_spec_2_3.md), rulings 2.5:G88-G128 in the patch's order. Amended rulings are marked amended_by, superseded ones superseded_by; a ruling example that no longer holds is archived. Function-word rows, slot notes, the clause and noun-phrase templates, the valency pattern and the motion-prefix rule follow; antizi is added; the -ti items leave the derivations; examples fixed by the patch's audits (commands, po viki, tonsi, ka for present location).

Liraasa 2.5, step 3: the housekeeping the author approved: I-26 (2.3:G73's album example archived), I-27 (time words classed, duplicates marked), I-33 (one wording for ne's scope), I-40 (examples classed as canonical, illustration or contrast), I-41 (ATTITUDE words), I-44 (historical and formulae rows; obsolete digit comments archived). I-02 and I-52 are summaries, changed in the build scripts.

changesets_3_0.summary: Liraasa 3.0, "Devotion, Music and Measure" (ADR-0021), from the author's 3.0 patch. PROPOSED: PROPOSED: every entry requires the author's ratification before it becomes canon. Additions only: rulings 3.0:G129-G141; the vocative iya; 15 roots and 112 compounds; 17 listed derivations and 1 lexicalised diminutive; 33 restored forms on 2.5 headwords; the clause template, its edges and the miyo, sela and gagu rows follow the rulings.
